lead: Contiguous memory allocation gives each process one continuous block of physical memory. The idea is simple: a process starts at one address and grows upward, with no gaps inside its block. Fixed partitions, made at boot, waste space inside a partition. Variable partitions create free holes at run time. The OS must choose a hole for every new process using first fit, best fit, worst fit or next fit. The choice decides how much memory is wasted. This scheme is the baseline that paging and segmentation improve on.
prereq: You need 4.1 for base and limit, and 4.2 for what happens when no hole is big enough.

blocks.text: In variable partitioning, the OS does not pre-cut memory. It starts with one large free block. When a process arrives, the OS takes a hole—a continuous free block—large enough for it and gives the process the first part. The rest of the hole stays free. When the process exits, its block becomes a hole again. The OS merges that hole with any free neighbours, so two adjacent holes become one bigger hole. Without merging, memory breaks into many small pieces.

items: First fit: scan holes from the start and take the first hole that fits.
Best fit: scan all holes and take the smallest hole that fits.
Worst fit: scan all holes and take the largest hole that fits.
Next fit: like first fit, but resume scanning from the hole after the last placement, not from the start.

blocks.where: leftover is the free space left in the chosen hole, in KB here; hole size and request size are also in KB. The formula applies only when hole size ≥ request size.

blocks.text: In fixed partitioning, the OS cuts memory into a fixed number of partitions at boot. The partition sizes stay fixed for the life of the system. A process must fit completely inside one partition. If a 300 KB process sits in a 512 KB partition, 212 KB inside that partition is wasted. This waste is internal fragmentation: the unused space is inside the allocated block. The process cannot share the leftover with another process. The number of partitions limits how many processes can be in memory at once. Some systems use unequal partitions to fit common process sizes. Fixed partitions are simple and need no hole search, but every process that does not fill its partition pays the waste.

sections.h3: External fragmentation, compaction and the 50-percent rule

blocks.text: Variable partitions avoid internal waste but create external fragmentation. Free memory is split into holes between allocated blocks. Total free memory may be large enough for a new process, yet no single hole is big enough, so the process waits even though memory is free. Compaction fixes this by sliding allocated blocks together, leaving one large hole. Moving a running process changes its physical addresses. Compaction therefore needs execution-time relocation: the CPU must translate every logical address to a physical address at run time, and the OS updates the process's base register after the move. A program that uses absolute physical addresses cannot be moved safely.

The 50-percent rule is a rule of thumb for first fit. Over a long run, with many processes arriving and leaving, about half of memory ends up in holes, on average, and half in allocated blocks. The number of holes grows too, so searching takes longer. The rule is an average, not a limit. Fixed-size blocks, covered in 4.4, remove external fragmentation by allowing any free frame to hold any page. Variable-length logical pieces in 4.6 face a related placement problem.

examples.question: Free holes in address order are 100 KB, 500 KB, 200 KB, 300 KB and 600 KB. Requests arrive in this order: 212 KB, 417 KB, 112 KB and 426 KB. For first fit, best fit and worst fit, show the hole used by each request, the leftover after each successful placement, and whether every request is placed.
steps: First fit, 212 KB: 100 is too small; 500 fits. Take 500. Leftover = 500 − 212 = 288 KB. H = [100, 288, 200, 300, 600] KB.
First fit, 417 KB: 100, 288, 200 and 300 are too small; 600 fits. Take 600. Leftover = 600 − 417 = 183 KB. H = [100, 288, 200, 300, 183] KB.
First fit, 112 KB: 100 is too small; 288 fits. Take 288. Leftover = 288 − 112 = 176 KB. H = [100, 176, 200, 300, 183] KB.
First fit, 426 KB: largest hole is 300 KB, which is less than 426 KB. No hole fits; request waits.
Best fit, 212 KB: fitting holes are 300, 500 and 600; smallest is 300. Take 300. Leftover = 300 − 212 = 88 KB. H = [100, 500, 200, 88, 600] KB.
Best fit, 417 KB: fitting holes are 500 and 600; smallest is 500. Take 500. Leftover = 500 − 417 = 83 KB. H = [100, 83, 200, 88, 600] KB.
Best fit, 112 KB: fitting holes are 200 and 600; smallest is 200. Take 200. Leftover = 200 − 112 = 88 KB. H = [100, 83, 88, 88, 600] KB.
Best fit, 426 KB: 600 fits. Take 600. Leftover = 600 − 426 = 174 KB. H = [100, 83, 88, 88, 174] KB. All four requests are placed.
Worst fit, 212 KB: largest hole is 600. Take 600. Leftover = 600 − 212 = 388 KB. H = [100, 500, 200, 300, 388] KB.
Worst fit, 417 KB: largest fitting hole is 500; 388 is too small. Take 500. Leftover = 500 − 417 = 83 KB. H = [100, 83, 200, 300, 388] KB.
Worst fit, 112 KB: largest hole is 388. Take 388. Leftover = 388 − 112 = 276 KB. H = [100, 83, 200, 300, 276] KB.
Worst fit, 426 KB: largest hole is 300 KB, which is less than 426 KB. No hole fits; request waits.
examples.answer: First fit places 212, 417 and 112 KB and leaves leftovers 288, 183 and 176 KB; best fit places all four and leaves 88, 83, 88 and 174 KB; worst fit places 212, 417 and 112 KB and leaves 388, 83 and 276 KB. All values are in KB.

traps: Best fit is not always the best overall. It leaves the smallest leftovers, which often become tiny holes too small to use.
External fragmentation is holes between allocated blocks, in variable partitions. Internal fragmentation is waste inside a fixed partition or the last page of a process.
Next fit does not rescan from the start; it continues from the hole after the last placement, so its holes chosen can differ from first fit.
Compaction needs execution-time relocation. Moving a process is safe only if its addresses are translated at run time and its base register is updated.
The 50-percent rule is an average for first fit, not a rule that half of RAM must stay free or a fixed limit.

quiz.q: Define a hole in variable partitioning.
quiz.a: A hole is a continuous free block of physical memory.

quiz.q: Why does fixed partitioning cause internal fragmentation?
quiz.a: A process smaller than its partition leaves unused space inside the allocated partition, and no other process can use that space.

quiz.q: Holes are 200 KB, 450 KB and 300 KB. A request of 250 KB arrives. Which hole does best fit choose, and what is the leftover?
quiz.a: Best fit takes the smallest hole that fits: 300 KB. Leftover = 300 − 250 = 50 KB.

quiz.q: Total free memory is 800 KB, in holes of 300 KB, 300 KB and 200 KB. A 500 KB request waits. Why?
quiz.a: This is external fragmentation. No single hole is at least 500 KB, even though the total free memory is 800 KB.

quiz.q: What does next fit change compared with first fit?
quiz.a: Next fit resumes the scan from the hole after the last placement, instead of restarting from the first hole.

quiz.q: First fit with holes 100 KB, 500 KB and 200 KB. Requests are 150 KB then 300 KB. Show the placements and leftovers.
quiz.a: 150 KB takes 500 KB, leaving 350 KB. Holes become 100, 350 and 200 KB. 300 KB takes 350 KB, leaving 50 KB. Holes become 100, 50 and 200 KB.

quiz.q: Compaction can remove external fragmentation. Give one hardware or OS condition and one program condition needed for safe compaction.
quiz.a: The CPU must translate logical addresses to physical addresses at run time, and the OS must update the base register after moving a process. The program must not use absolute physical addresses.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real kernels rarely use pure contiguous allocation for user processes; they use paging plus allocators such as buddy and slab. The same fragmentation question appears inside the kernel heap and in long-running servers, where small holes can stop a large allocation. Compaction reappears in garbage-collected runtimes and in memory defragmentation for virtual machines. Search for buddy allocator fragmentation, slab allocator, and execution-time relocation.
